brief: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky, via Zero Hedge, flags rising dispersion in tech/semis as an echo of Jan-March 2000. The SOX is ~14% below its June highs while only three constituents sit closer to their own highs than the index does; 10 of 30 names are over 30% off highs and the average is off ~26%. Krinsky's parallel: the SOX peaked March 14, 2000, and 13 of the 20 current constituents that existed then made 52-week highs after that peak, so single names can keep rallying after the index tops. He reiterates that bullish investors should favor names near new highs over laggards. Separately, a QQQ moving-average reversal signal from last Thursday has historically produced positive 5-day returns (median +1.13%, 73% win rate) that flip negative 30-40 days out, though precedent (2007, 2011, 2015) shows a new high can still come first; QQQ is up ~4% and near a new high, though under 60% of NDX names sit above their 200-day average. SPX shows six straight days of more 52-week lows than highs and negative breadth (9 of 11 sectors) even as it nears highs, while BKX is over 10% below its 30-day high, a breadth-versus-price gap last seen in January 2000.
